papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: Neuron Specialization: Leveraging intrinsic task modularity for multilingual machine translation
papers.research_question: How do neurons in multilingual translation models exhibit language-specific modularity, and can this be leveraged to reduce interference and improve translation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that FFN neurons in multilingual models exhibit language-specific modularity, and introduces Neuron Specialization, a method that leverages this to reduce interference and improve translation performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that intrinsic modularity in multilingual models can be leveraged to improve translation performance by reducing interference and enhancing transfer, with Neuron Specialization providing consistent gains.
papers.key_findings:
FFN neurons in multilingual translation models activate in a language-specific way, with overlaps indicating linguistic proximity.
The specialization of neurons evolves across layers, becoming more language-agnostic in the encoder and more specific in the decoder.
The proposed Neuron Specialization method, which updates task-specific neurons via sparse networks, consistently improves translation quality over baselines.
This method effectively reduces negative interference in high-resource languages and boosts knowledge transfer in low-resource languages.
Neuron Specialization is efficient, requiring minimal extra parameters and time compared to adapter-based methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to multilingual machine translation and does not explore other multilingual NLP tasks.
Analysis is confined to feed-forward network components, excluding other Transformer elements like attention mechanisms.
Neuron identification relies on ReLU activation states; other activation functions like GELU are not considered.
future_direction: Extend the exploration to a broader range of Multilingual Natural Language Processing tasks beyond translation.
Investigate the modularity of other Transformer components such as attention mechanisms or layer normalization.
Explore neuron specialization for FFNs using activation functions other than ReLU, such as GELU.
papers.abstract: Training a unified multilingual model promotes knowledge transfer but inevitably introduces negative interference. Language-specific modeling methods show promise in reducing interference. However, they often rely on heuristics to distribute capacity and struggle to foster cross-lingual transfer via isolated modules. In this paper, we explore intrinsic task modularity within multilingual networks and leverage these observations to circumvent interference under multilingual translation. We show that neurons in the feed-forward layers tend to be activated in a language-specific manner. Meanwhile, these specialized neurons exhibit structural overlaps that reflect language proximity, which progress across layers. Based on these findings, we propose Neuron Specialization, an approach that identifies specialized neurons to modularize feed-forward layers and then continuously updates them through sparse networks. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves consistent performance gains over strong baselines with additional analyses demonstrating reduced interference and increased knowledge transfer.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: How Likely Do LLMs with CoT Mimic Human Reasoning?
papers.research_question: How do LLMs with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) compare to human reasoning in terms of causal structure between instruction, reasoning steps, and answers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs with CoT often deviate from ideal causal chains, showing spurious correlations; in-context learning strengthens causal structure, while supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning weaken it.
papers.conclusion: LLMs with CoT do not always mimic human reasoning perfectly, indicating a need for new techniques to improve reasoning processes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit four types of Structural Causal Models (SCMs): causal chain, common cause, full connection, and isolation.
Spurious correlations between instruction and answer lead to consistency errors and unfaithful reasoning.
In-context learning (ICL) strengthens the causal structure, but supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) weaken it.
Larger model size does not necessarily lead to stronger causal structures or better reasoning.
The type of SCM predicts the likelihood of consistency errors and faithfulness in reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Focus on basic CoT, leaving analysis of advanced methods like tree-of-thought for future work.
Coarse-grained analysis with only three variables; fine-grained structures are not considered.
future_direction: Analysis of advanced CoT methods such as tree-of-thought and graph-of-thought.
More detailed analysis of fine-grained reasoning structures.
Enhancing causal structures in LLMs during training using counterfactual examples or causal regulation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought emerges as a promising technique for eliciting reasoning capabilities from Large Language Models (LLMs). However, it does not always improve task performance or accurately represent reasoning processes, leaving unresolved questions about its usage. In this paper, we diagnose the underlying mechanism by comparing the reasoning process of LLMs with humans, using causal analysis to understand the relationships between the problem instruction, reasoning, and the answer in LLMs. Our empirical study reveals that LLMs often deviate from the ideal causal chain, resulting in spurious correlations and potential consistency errors (inconsistent reasoning and answers). We also examine various factors influencing the causal structure, finding that in-context learning with examples strengthens it, while post-training techniques like supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on human feedback weaken it. To our surprise, the causal structure cannot be strengthened by enlarging the model size only, urging research on new techniques. We hope that this preliminary study will shed light on understanding and improving the reasoning process in LLM.

papers.title: Unlocking Multilingual Reasoning Capability of LLMs and LVLMs through Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How to enhance multilingual reasoning capabilities of LLMs and LVLMs without additional training or external tools?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MRRE, a training-free inference-time method that enhances multilingual reasoning in LLMs and LVLMs by steering hidden states with precomputed vectors.
papers.conclusion: Proposes MRRE, a training-free inference-time method that enhances multilingual reasoning in LLMs and LVLMs, with comprehensive results demonstrating effectiveness and generalizability.
papers.key_findings:
MRRE improves non-English reasoning by an average of 5.48% and up to 7.54% in low-resource languages.
MRRE improves input-output language consistency by 3.78%.
MRRE is effective across both LLMs and LVLMs and across different benchmarks.
The method works by aligning non-English hidden states to English in middle layers and then restoring target language in later layers.
The vectors can be generalized across modalities (from LLM to LVLM).
papers.limitation:
MRRE requires access to internal representations, making it infeasible for closed-source models.
Experiments are limited to widely used benchmarks and models due to cost and resource constraints.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning capabilities, yet their performance in English significantly outperforms that in low-resource languages, raising fairness concerns in multilingual applications. Existing approaches either rely on costly multilingual training or employ prompting with external translation tools, both of which are resource-intensive and sensitive to translation quality. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free inference-time method to enhance Multilingual Reasoning capabilities via Representation Engineering (MRRE) without using any additional training data or tools. MRRE sequentially injects two precomputed vectors at specific layers during inference processing: cross-lingual reasoning enhancement vectors, which steer non-English reasoning representations toward English space to unlock multilingual reasoning, and target-language output anchoring vectors, which restore the distribution of the target language to preserve input-output language consistency. Comprehensive experiments across six advanced LLMs and LVLMs on four reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MRRE consistently enhances non-English reasoning by an average gain of 5.48% and up to 7.54% in low-resource languages (Thai and Swahili), while improving input-output language consistency by 3.78%.

papers.title: Sharing Matters: Analysing Neurons Across Languages and Tasks in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is neuron activation shared across tasks and languages in multilingual large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a fine-grained neuron classification method for multilingual LLMs and demonstrates that neurons shared across all languages (all-shared neurons) are crucial for model performance and generating accurate responses.
papers.conclusion: The study improves understanding of the internal workings of multilingual LLMs by showing the pivotal role of cross-lingually shared neurons and the task- and model-dependent nature of neuron activation patterns, paving the way for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating all-shared neurons significantly decreases model performance across tasks (up to 87.39% drop in accuracy).
All-shared neurons have the greatest impact on generating both answers and correct answers, as measured by Generation Impact Score and Correctness Impact Score.
Neuron activation patterns vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages; for example, instruction-finetuned models show more all-shared neurons than foundation models.
Neuron sharing does not always align with language similarity; languages from the same family do not necessarily share more neurons.
Deactivating certain neuron types (partial-shared or specific) can occasionally improve performance for some languages, possibly due to mitigating knowledge conflicts.
future_direction: More in-depth investigation of how factual knowledge is stored and shared across languages in LLMs.
Further exploration of the relationship between language similarity and neuron sharing.
Investigation of whether in-context learning leads to better neuron activation composition rather than invoking more neurons.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), and recent studies have aimed to understand their underlying mechanisms. However, most of this research is conducted within a monolingual setting, primarily focusing on English. Few studies have attempted to explore the internal workings of LLMs in multilingual settings. In this study, we aim to fill this research gap by examining how neuron activation is shared across tasks and languages. We classify neurons into four distinct categories based on their responses to a specific input across different languages: all-shared, partial-shared, specific, and non-activated. Building upon this categorisation, we conduct extensive experiments on three tasks across nine languages using several LLMs and present an in-depth analysis in this work. Our findings reveal that: (i) deactivating the all-shared neurons significantly decreases performance; (ii) the shared neurons play a vital role in generating responses, especially for the all-shared neurons; (iii) neuron activation patterns are highly sensitive and vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages. These findings shed light on the internal workings of multilingual LLMs and pave the way for future research. We release the code to foster research in this area.

papers.title: Understanding Chain-of-Thought in LLMs through Information Theory
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the quality of each step in a model's Chain-of-Thought reasoning without requiring annotated step-by-step data, in order to identify failure modes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information-theoretic framework to quantify the 'information-gain' at each step of a Chain-of-Thought reasoning process, enabling the identification of reasoning failures without the need for expensive annotated step-by-step data.
papers.conclusion: The information-theoretic framework provides a rigorous and practical method for evaluating Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs, enabling granular failure detection without the need for costly annotated data.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Information-Gain method accurately identifies incorrect reasoning steps in Chain-of-Thought, outperforming baseline methods like Outcome Reward Modeling and Math-Shepherd.
The method is effective in detecting errors even when the correctness of a step depends on previous steps, a scenario where baselines fail.
It does not require annotated Chain-of-Thought data, making it more scalable than process-based supervision methods.
The framework is validated on synthetic data, GSM8K, and PRM800k datasets, showing consistent performance across different complexities.
The information-gain metric can be applied to both linear and exploratory (e.g., O1/R1-style) reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance in complex reasoning tasks through the use of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, allowing models to break down problems into manageable sub-tasks. However, existing CoT evaluation techniques either require annotated CoT data or fall short in accurately assessing intermediate reasoning steps, leading to high rates of false positives. In this paper, we formalize CoT reasoning in LLMs through an information-theoretic lens. Specifically, our framework quantifies the `information-gain' at each reasoning step, enabling the identification of failure modes in LLMs without the need for expensive annotated datasets. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on toy arithmetic, GSM8K and PRM800k datasets, where it significantly outperforms existing outcome-based methods by providing more accurate insights into model performance on individual subtasks.

papers.title: Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models (LLMs) reason via chain-of-thought prompting, and do they rely on simple heuristics rather than genuine reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the PRONTO QA dataset and uses formal analysis to show that LLMs are capable of correct individual deduction steps but struggle with proof planning when multiple valid steps are available.
papers.conclusion: While the largest LLMs are generally capable of reasoning, they have difficulty with proof planning and selecting the correct proof step when multiple options are available.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are capable of making valid individual proof steps, even in fictional contexts.
LLMs have difficulty with proof planning: when multiple valid proof steps are available, they often select the wrong step, leading to incomplete proofs.
Real-world knowledge helps reasoning: performance is significantly better with true ontologies compared to fictional or false ones.
Longer proofs (5 hops) are challenging, especially with top-down traversal of the ontology.
For larger models, the main source of error is misleading steps rather than invalid steps.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to modus ponens, proof lengths of at most 5, and semantically simple sentences.
future_direction: Use PRONTO QA to compare LLM reasoning with human reasoning and explore which aspects of human reasoning LLMs acquired.
Develop reasoning systems with more sophisticated proof planning/search strategies, such as neurosymbolic approaches.
Investigate whether LLMs can produce longer proofs, reason with other deduction rules, or handle more semantically complex sentences.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable reasoning capabilities given chain-of-thought prompts (examples with intermediate reasoning steps). Existing benchmarks measure reasoning ability indirectly, by evaluating accuracy on downstream tasks such as mathematical reasoning. However, it is unclear how these models obtain the answers and whether they rely on simple heuristics rather than the generated chain-of-thought. To enable systematic exploration of the reasoning ability of LLMs, we present a new synthetic question-answering dataset called PrOntoQA, where each example is generated from a synthetic world model represented in first-order logic. This allows us to parse the generated chain-of-thought into symbolic proofs for formal analysis. Our analysis on InstructGPT and GPT-3 shows that LLMs are quite capable of making correct individual deduction steps, and so are generally capable of reasoning, even in fictional contexts. However, they have difficulty with proof planning: When multiple valid deduction steps are available, they are not able to systematically explore the different options.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of a Transformer Trained on a Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Task
papers.research_question: How does a transformer internally perform a symbolic multi-step reasoning task, specifically pathfinding in trees?
papers.core_contribution: The transformer implements a backward chaining algorithm for pathfinding, using deduction heads to climb the tree one level per layer, parallel computation via register tokens, and a one-step lookahead heuristic.
papers.conclusion: The transformer demonstrates deductive reasoning up to a certain depth, using parallelized strategies and heuristics, which provides insights into the operating principles of transformers for reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The first layer attention head concatenates edge tokens by copying source node information to target node positions.
Deduction heads in subsequent layers perform backward chaining, moving one step up the tree per layer.
For paths longer than the number of layers, the model uses register tokens to perform parallel backward chaining from multiple subgoals and merges subpaths.
The model uses a one-step lookahead heuristic to identify child nodes and avoid leaf nodes when backward chaining is insufficient.
The model's reasoning is depth-bounded and resorts to heuristics beyond its depth limit.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a synthetic symbolic reasoning task and may not directly translate to natural language tasks.
The input format uses shuffled edge lists in backward order, and the mechanisms might vary for other arrangements.
papers.abstract: Transformers demonstrate impressive performance on a range of reasoning benchmarks. To evaluate the degree to which these abilities are a result of actual reasoning, existing work has focused on developing sophisticated benchmarks for behavioral studies. However, these studies do not provide insights into the internal mechanisms driving the observed capabilities. To improve our understanding of the internal mechanisms of transformers, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of a transformer trained on a synthetic reasoning task. We identify a set of interpretable mechanisms the model uses to solve the task, and validate our findings using correlational and causal evidence. Our results suggest that it implements a depth-bounded recurrent mechanisms that operates in parallel and stores intermediate results in selected token positions. We anticipate that the motifs we identified in our synthetic setting can provide valuable insights into the broader operating principles of transformers and thus provide a basis for understanding more complex models.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
papers.research_question: Does reasoning require large depth but not necessarily many parameters, and can looped models effectively solve reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Looped transformers can solve reasoning tasks with fewer parameters by providing depth through looping, and they exhibit an inductive bias towards reasoning over memorization.
papers.conclusion: Looped models are effective for reasoning tasks, providing depth without many parameters, and have an inductive bias towards improving reasoning performance over memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Looped models nearly match the performance of non-looped models with the same depth on synthetic reasoning tasks like addition, p-hop induction, and i-GSM, despite having fewer parameters.
For language modeling, looped models have worse perplexity but better reasoning performance on downstream tasks compared to non-looped models with the same FLOPs.
Looped models show scaling behavior with effective depth similar to chain-of-thought reasoning.
Theoretically, looped models can simulate iterative algorithms and chain-of-thought reasoning.
A regularization method that encourages layer similarity inherits the inductive bias of looped models towards reasoning.
papers.limitation: The results are limited to the tested reasoning problems and may not generalize to other forms of reasoning (e.g., multimodal and common-sense reasoning).
future_direction: Generalizing the results to other forms of reasoning such as multimodal and common-sense reasoning.
Formalizing reasoning problems more succinctly.
Further exploration of the inductive bias towards reasoning at the same perplexity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have shown remarkable reasoning abilities and scaling laws suggest that large parameter count, especially along the depth axis, is the primary driver. In this work, we make a stronger claim -- many reasoning problems require a large depth but not necessarily many parameters. This unlocks a novel application of looped models for reasoning. Firstly, we show that for many synthetic reasoning problems like addition, $p$-hop induction, and math problems, a $k$-layer transformer looped $L$ times nearly matches the performance of a $kL$-layer non-looped model, and is significantly better than a $k$-layer model. This is further corroborated by theoretical results showing that many such reasoning problems can be solved via iterative algorithms, and thus, can be solved effectively using looped models with nearly optimal depth. Perhaps surprisingly, these benefits also translate to practical settings of language modeling -- on many downstream reasoning tasks, a language model with $k$-layers looped $L$ times can be competitive to, if not better than, a $kL$-layer language model. In fact, our empirical analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon: looped and non-looped models exhibit scaling behavior that depends on their effective depth, akin to the inference-time scaling of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. We further elucidate the connection to CoT reasoning by proving that looped models implicitly generate latent thoughts and can simulate $T$ steps of CoT with $T$ loops. Inspired by these findings, we also present an interesting dichotomy between reasoning and memorization, and design a looping-based regularization that is effective on both fronts.

papers.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms behind Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and how does it unlock the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) for mathematical and reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper theoretically proves that bounded-depth Transformers without Chain-of-Thought (CoT) require super-polynomial size to solve basic mathematical tasks, while constant-size autoregressive Transformers with CoT can solve them, and extends this to show CoT enables solving dynamic programming problems.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought is the key to unlocking the reasoning capabilities of autoregressive Transformers, both theoretically and empirically, by allowing step-by-step generation that overcomes the expressivity limitations of bounded-depth models.
papers.key_findings:
Bounded-depth log-precision Transformers of polynomial size cannot directly solve arithmetic and linear equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with input length.
Autoregressive Transformers of constant depth and size can generate correct CoT solutions for arithmetic and linear equation tasks.
LLMs with CoT can solve a general class of decision-making problems formulated as dynamic programming.
Experimental results show Transformers fail to directly predict answers but consistently learn to generate correct step-by-step CoT solutions given sufficient demonstrations.
CoT increases the effective depth of the Transformer circuit, allowing it to solve problems beyond the TC0 complexity class.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have discovered that Chain-of-Thought prompting (CoT) can dramatically improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when dealing with complex tasks involving mathematics or reasoning. Despite the enormous empirical success, the underlying mechanisms behind CoT and how it unlocks the potential of LLMs remain elusive. In this paper, we take a first step towards theoretically answering these questions. Specifically, we examine the expressivity of LLMs with CoT in solving fundamental mathematical and decision-making problems. By using circuit complexity theory, we first give impossibility results showing that bounded-depth Transformers are unable to directly produce correct answers for basic arithmetic/equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with respect to the input length. In contrast, we then prove by construction that autoregressive Transformers of constant size suffice to solve both tasks by generating CoT derivations using a commonly used math language format. Moreover, we show LLMs with CoT can handle a general class of decision-making problems known as Dynamic Programming, thus justifying its power in tackling complex real-world tasks. Finally, an extensive set of experiments show that, while Transformers always fail to directly predict the answers, they can consistently learn to generate correct solutions step-by-step given sufficient CoT demonstrations.

papers.title: Eliciting Chain-of-Thought in Base LLMs via Gradient-Based Representation Optimization
papers.research_question: Can we solely manipulate the hidden states to elicit CoT reasoning from a base LLM, without distorting its language quality?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a gradient-based hidden state optimization method to elicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning in base LLMs, using a balanced likelihood and prior regularization framework to guide hidden states toward reasoning while preserving language quality.
papers.conclusion: Presents a principled gradient-based activation optimization method to elicit CoT reasoning from base LLMs, grounded in probabilistic generation theory, which balances likelihood and prior terms to activate reasoning without distribution shift, and consistently outperforms vector arithmetic methods.
papers.key_findings:
Our method consistently outperforms existing hidden state steering methods across diverse reasoning benchmarks.
The method unlocks latent reasoning capabilities in base LLMs without additional training.
The optimization framework balances reasoning effectiveness and linguistic fluency.
The method is effective across multiple LLM architectures (Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, Phi).
The method's performance depends on the choice of hidden states and layers, with middle layers showing better classification performance.
papers.limitation:
The method can only unlock intrinsic reasoning abilities and cannot inject new capabilities; for models with limited intrinsic reasoning capacity, it cannot create non-existent capabilities.
The method's effectiveness depends on the classification performance and layer selection; improper choices may lead to suboptimal results.
future_direction: Integrating the method with post-training techniques to further amplify reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is a critical capability for large language models (LLMs), enabling them to tackle com- plex multi-step tasks. While base LLMs, pre-trained on general text corpora, often struggle with reasoning due to a lack of specialized training, recent studies reveal their latent reason- ing potential tied to hidden states. However, existing hidden state manipulation methods, such as linear activation steering, suffer from limitations due to their rigid and unconstrained nature, often leading to distribution shifts and degraded text quality. In this work, we propose a novel approach for elic- iting CoT reasoning from base LLMs through hidden state manipulation grounded in probabilistic conditional generation. By reformulating the challenge as an optimization problem with a balanced likelihood and prior regularization framework, our method guides hidden states toward reasoning-oriented trajectories while preserving linguistic coherence. Extensive evaluations across mathematical, commonsense, and logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our approach con- sistently outperforms existing steering methods, offering a theoretically principled and effective solution for enhancing reasoning capabilities in base LLMs.

papers.title: Multi-head Transformers Provably Learn Symbolic Multi-step Reasoning via Gradient Descent
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn to solve symbolic multi-step reasoning problems via chain-of-thought processes, specifically path-finding in trees, through gradient descent training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that one-layer multi-head transformers can learn symbolic multi-step reasoning via chain-of-thought through gradient descent, with attention heads specializing and coordinating to solve path-finding tasks, and provides generalization guarantees to unseen trees.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that one-layer multi-head transformers can learn symbolic multi-step reasoning via chain-of-thought with provable optimization and generalization guarantees, offering mechanistic insights into how transformers implement algorithmic procedures.
papers.key_findings:
One-layer transformers can learn to solve backward and forward path-finding tasks in trees via chain-of-thought reasoning.
Multi-head attention heads autonomously specialize and coordinate to handle multi-stage reasoning, with one head performing path-finding and another controlling stage transitions.
Gradient descent training dynamics converge to parameters that implement the desired reasoning mechanisms.
The learned models generalize to unseen tree structures, learning generalizable rules rather than memorizing paths.
Extending reasoning length via chain-of-thought allows shallow transformers to solve complex tasks that might otherwise require deeper architectures.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in multi-step reasoning tasks. However, understandings of the underlying mechanisms by which they acquire these abilities through training remain limited, particularly from a theoretical standpoint. This work investigates how transformers learn to solve symbolic multi-step reasoning problems through chain-of-thought processes, focusing on path-finding in trees. We analyze two intertwined tasks: a backward reasoning task, where the model outputs a path from a goal node to the root, and a more complex forward reasoning task, where the model implements two-stage reasoning by first identifying the goal-to-root path and then reversing it to produce the root-to-goal path. Our theoretical analysis, grounded in the dynamics of gradient descent, shows that trained one-layer transformers can provably solve both tasks with generalization guarantees to unseen trees. In particular, our multi-phase training dynamics for forward reasoning elucidate how different attention heads learn to specialize and coordinate autonomously to solve the two subtasks in a single autoregressive path. These results provide a mechanistic explanation of how trained transformers can implement sequential algorithmic procedures. Moreover, they offer insights into the emergence of reasoning abilities, suggesting that when tasks are structured to take intermediate chain-of-thought steps, even shallow multi-head transformers can effectively solve problems that would otherwise require deeper architectures.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Placing language in an integrated understanding system: Next steps toward human-level performance in neural language models
papers.research_question: What is the role of language in human intelligence and how can we extend current machine language models to achieve human-level language understanding by integrating language with other modalities and memory systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework for building an integrated understanding system that combines insights from cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence, using query-based attention and memory systems to extend current language models toward human-level language understanding.
papers.conclusion: Combining insights from neuroscience and AI will take us closer to human-level language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Current language models are limited by their focus on language-internal tasks and lack of memory for remote information.
The human brain integrates language with other modalities and uses complementary learning systems (neocortex and medial temporal lobe) for understanding.
Query-based attention is a key innovation that can be extended to integrate multiple modalities and memory.
Future models should incorporate an MTL-like memory to handle remote information and improve data efficiency.
Understanding should be seen as constructing situation representations, which are compositional and grounded in multi-sensory experience.
papers.limitation: The proposed sketch leaves important issues open and will require substantial development.
future_direction: Incorporating an MTL-like memory to allow the use of remote information beyond the current episode.
Integrating a frontal lobe-like subsystem to guide processing according to task demands.
Extending the approach beyond concrete situations to abstract ones involving laws, belief systems, and scientific theories.
papers.abstract: Language is crucial for human intelligence, but what exactly is its role? We take language to be a part of a system for understanding and communicating about situations. In humans, these abilities emerge gradually from experience and depend on domain-general principles of biological neural networks: connection-based learning, distributed representation, and context-sensitive, mutual constraint satisfaction-based processing. Current artificial language processing systems rely on the same domain general principles, embodied in artificial neural networks. Indeed, recent progress in this field depends on query-based attention, which extends the ability of these systems to exploit context and has contributed to remarkable breakthroughs. Nevertheless, most current models focus exclusively on language-internal tasks, limiting their ability to perform tasks that depend on understanding situations. These systems also lack memory for the contents of prior situations outside of a fixed contextual span. We describe the organization of the brain's distributed understanding system, which includes a fast learning system that addresses the memory problem. We sketch a framework for future models of understanding drawing equally on cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence and exploiting query-based attention. We highlight relevant current directions and consider further developments needed to fully capture human-level language understanding in a computational system.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Words ? Exploring framework for hidden state reasoning
papers.research_question: Can reasoning in a continuous latent space, as opposed to the language space, lead to more efficient and effective reasoning in LLMs, particularly for tasks requiring planning and search?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Coconut, a method for reasoning in a continuous latent space by feeding the last hidden state back as the next input embedding, which enables emergent tree search behavior and improves reasoning efficiency and accuracy on certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in latent space leads to advanced emergent behaviors like BFS, and Coconut enhances LLM performance across reasoning tasks, with potential for future scaling and research.
papers.key_findings:
Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require planning and search (ProsQA).
Continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, enabling a breadth-first search (BFS) pattern.
Coconut provides a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency (fewer tokens) compared to CoT.
The multi-stage training curriculum is crucial for learning latent reasoning; without it, performance drops.
Increasing the number of continuous thoughts per reasoning step (c) can improve performance up to a point.
papers.limitation:
Training requires a multi-stage curriculum; without it, performance drops significantly.
Larger models (Llama) show less pronounced gains, possibly due to extensive language-focused pre-training.
Training efficiency is challenging due to sequential forward passes, limiting parallelism.
future_direction: Refine and scale latent reasoning to pretraining for better generalization.
Combine iCoT and Coconut for improved training.
Develop better strategies for learning reasoning in latent space without supervision from language reasoning chains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically constrained to reason in the language space, where they express the reasoning process through a chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems. However, the language space may not always be optimal for reasoning. Most word tokens primarily ensure textual coherence and are not essential for reasoning, while some critical tokens require complex planning and pose challenges to LLMs. To explore the potential of reasoning beyond language, we introduce a new paradigm called Coconut (Chain of Continuous Thought). Coconut utilizes the last hidden state of the LLM as a representation of the reasoning state, termed "continuous thought." Instead of decoding this state into words, we feed it back to the model as the next input embedding directly in the continuous space. This latent reasoning paradigm enables an advanced reasoning pattern, where continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, allowing the model to perform a breadth-first search (BFS) rather than committing prematurely to a single deterministic path as in CoT. Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require substantial search during planning and achieves a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models perform multi-step reasoning tasks by using a reasoning mechanism or by memorizing answers from pretraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that LMs perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning trees can often be detected from LM attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA for most examples.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that contribute to reasoning tree detection degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with higher model accuracy and robustness to noise.
Finetuned models show clearer reasoning patterns in attention than few-shot models.
papers.limitation:
The study considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
The analysis averages over attention heads, but heads may have different functions, especially in shallow models.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought reasoning.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Yifan Hou, Jiaoda Li, Yu Fei, Alessandro Stolfo, Wangchunshu Zhou, Guangtao Zeng, Antoine Bosselut, Mrinmaya Sachan. Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2023.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Chain-of-Thought Prompting: An Empirical Study of What Matters
papers.research_question: What makes Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting effective and which aspects of the demonstrated reasoning steps contribute to its performance? Specifically, are ground truth bridging objects/language templates important, and if not, what are the key aspects needed for the LLM to reason properly?
papers.core_contribution: The validity of reasoning in Chain-of-Thought demonstrations is not crucial for performance; instead, the relevance of the rationale to the query and the coherence (correct ordering) of the reasoning steps are the key aspects that determine the effectiveness of CoT prompting.
papers.conclusion: The study deepens understanding of CoT prompting by showing that valid reasoning in demonstrations is not the primary driver of performance; instead, relevance and coherence are critical. This suggests LLMs' reasoning abilities largely come from pretraining, and CoT demonstrations mainly regularize the output format.
papers.key_findings:
Providing demonstrations with completely invalid reasoning steps can achieve over 80-90% of the performance of standard CoT prompting, indicating that logical validity in the examples is not essential.
Relevance (the rationale being based on the query) and coherence (the correct ordering of steps) are identified as the two key aspects for effective CoT prompting.
Relevance is more important than coherence for bridging objects (e.g., numbers, entities), while coherence of language templates is particularly important.
When both relevance and coherence are removed, performance drops significantly, sometimes below standard prompting without rationales.
The findings suggest LLMs may not be learning to reason from the demonstrations but rather using pretrained abilities, with CoT mainly specifying an output format that regularizes generation to be step-by-step, in order, and relevant.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to two types of reasoning tasks (arithmetic reasoning and multi-hop question answering); other tasks like symbolic reasoning were not studied due to their highly template-based nature.
The construction of invalid reasoning demonstrations was done manually, lacking a systematic treatment; automatically synthesizing such rationales is challenging.
Intrinsic evaluation relies on the correctness of bridging objects, which may not be a comprehensive metric and requires costly annotation.
future_direction: Extending the ablation designs to other types of reasoning tasks, such as symbolic reasoning tasks where steps have little variation.
Developing a more systematic treatment of the 'invalid reasoning' setting, e.g., by categorizing informal logical fallacies.
Improving intrinsic evaluation methods to be more comprehensive and reference-free.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting can dramatically improve the multi-step reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs). CoT explicitly encourages the LLM to generate intermediate rationales for solving a problem, by providing a series of reasoning steps in the demonstrations. Despite its success, there is still little understanding of what makes CoT prompting effective and which aspects of the demonstrated reasoning steps contribute to its performance. In this paper, we show that CoT reasoning is possible even with invalid demonstrations - prompting with invalid reasoning steps can achieve over 80-90% of the performance obtained using CoT under various metrics, while still generating coherent lines of reasoning during inference. Further experiments show that other aspects of the rationales, such as being relevant to the query and correctly ordering the reasoning steps, are much more important for effective CoT reasoning. Overall, these findings both deepen our understanding of CoT prompting, and open up new questions regarding LLMs' capability to learn to reason in context.

papers.title: Uncovering Intermediate Variables in Transformers using Circuit Probing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically uncover low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit probing, a method that combines probing and causal analysis to automatically uncover circuits computing hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Circuit probing provides a unified approach for a variety of analyses, combining and extending the capabilities of existing methods for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit probing can decipher the algorithms learned by models on simple arithmetic tasks.
Circuit probing reveals modular structure within a model, showing that shared and free variables are computed by distinct circuits.
Circuit probing tracks the development of circuits over training, showing circuit formation occurs continuously before generalization.
Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Triangulation as an Acceptance Rule for Multilingual Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we validate mechanistic explanations for multilingual models to ensure they are causal and invariant across languages and scripts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces triangulation, an acceptance rule for mechanistic interpretability that requires necessity, sufficiency, and invariance across predicate-preserving environments to filter spurious circuits.
papers.conclusion: Triangulation offers a concrete step toward rigorous, transferable mechanistic explanations by requiring cross-environment consistency, allowing circuits that pass to be interpreted with greater confidence as capturing language-agnostic mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.
Triangulation can be extended to multimodal settings by holding the image fixed and varying the prompt language.
Triangulation enables separation of circuits into visual, linguistic, and spurious categories based on cross-environment invariance.
The method is grounded in causal abstraction theory and provides an approximate transformation score over interchange interventions.
Triangulation requires explicit cue-only falsifiers to reject mechanisms that rely on surface cues rather than predicate information.
papers.limitation:
Multiple circuits may satisfy triangulation if their effects are redundant; triangulation identifies sufficient mechanisms but does not guarantee uniqueness.
The quality of reference families is decisive, and poor-quality families can mislead by either accepting spurious circuits or rejecting genuine circuits.
Causal interventions at scale are computationally expensive, and prioritization strategies are advisable for practical deployment.
When using LLM judges to verify predicate preservation, circularity risks arise if the judge correlates with the model under study.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models achieve strong aggregate performance yet often behave unpredictably across languages, scripts, and cultures. We argue that mechanistic explanations for such models should satisfy a \emph{causal} standard: claims must survive causal interventions and must \emph{cross-reference} across environments that perturb surface form while preserving meaning. We formalize \emph{reference families} as predicate-preserving variants and introduce \emph{triangulation}, an acceptance rule requiring necessity (ablating the circuit degrades the target behavior), sufficiency (patching activations transfers the behavior), and invariance (both effects remain directionally stable and of sufficient magnitude across the reference family). To supply candidate subgraphs, we adopt automatic circuit discovery and \emph{accept or reject} those candidates by triangulation. We ground triangulation in causal abstraction by casting it as an approximate transformation score over a distribution of interchange interventions, connect it to the pragmatic interpretability agenda, and present a comparative experimental protocol across multiple model families, language pairs, and tasks. Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.

papers.title: Visual Thoughts: A Unified Perspective of Understanding Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: Is there a unified explanation for why different multimodal chain-of-thought paradigms enhance large vision-language models in distinct ways?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves large vision-language models by incorporating visual thoughts, which act as an intermediate cache for visual information, enabling more efficient and effective reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Visual thoughts provide a unified perspective for understanding how multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning enhances large vision-language models, acting as visual caches that improve information flow and reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Removing visual thoughts from the reasoning process impairs model performance more than reasoning directly from the query alone.
Different expressions of visual thoughts (natural language, structured language, edited image, generative image) vary in effectiveness depending on task clarity and conciseness.
Visual thoughts serve as primary intermediaries, connecting input images to deeper transformer layers and facilitating advanced visual information processing.
Image-form visual thoughts consistently outperform text-form visual thoughts, especially in complex scenarios requiring detailed visual information.
Visual thoughts are more effective than simple image captions for conveying visual information in complex scenes, improving reasoning accuracy.
future_direction: Exploring the integration of multiple visual thoughts to enhance visual information transmission in multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved significant success in multimodal tasks, with multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) further enhancing performance and interpretability. Recent MCoT methods fall into two categories: (i) Textual-MCoT (T-MCoT), which takes multimodal input and produces textual output; and (ii) Interleaved-MCoT (I-MCoT), which generates interleaved image-text outputs. Despite advances in both approaches, the mechanisms driving these improvements are not fully understood. To fill this gap, we first reveal that MCoT boosts LVLMs by incorporating visual thoughts, which convey image information to the reasoning process regardless of the MCoT format, depending only on clarity and conciseness of expression. Furthermore, to explore visual thoughts systematically, we define four distinct forms of visual thought expressions and analyze them comprehensively. Our findings demonstrate that these forms differ in clarity and conciseness, yielding varying levels of MCoT improvement. Additionally, we explore the internal nature of visual thoughts, finding that visual thoughts serve as intermediaries between the input image and reasoning to deeper transformer layers, enabling more advanced visual information transmission. We hope that the visual thoughts can inspire further breakthroughs for future MCoT research.

papers.title: On the Representational Capacity of Neural Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
